name: Plaza de Armas
label: Plaza de Armas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Catedral Metropolitana de Santiago' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Catedral Metropolitana de Santiago de Chile' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10272414: 'Monumento a la Libertad Americana', the best-known feature inside 'Plaza de Armas de Santiago de Chile' (221 m across).
notes: The historic main square at the heart of Santiago.

text.description: Plaza de Armas is the main square of Santiago and the point from which the city grid was laid out. Pedro de Gamboa planned it in 1541, working for the founder Pedro de Valdivia. It photographs well because so much is gathered in one open space: palm trees, the Metropolitan Cathedral, the neoclassical Central Post Office, the Museo Histórico Nacional and the municipal building all face the square. In the middle stands the Monument to American Freedom, a Carrara marble allegory by Francesco Orselino. The present cathedral was built between 1748 and 1775, and Joaquín Toesca designed a new façade for it in 1780. The square and its surroundings were declared a national monument (a zona típica) in 1986. The best angle is from the cathedral's front stairways at the north-west corner of the square. From there the cathedral's façade sits in the foreground, with the palm-lined plaza and the colonial buildings opening out around it. Go in the morning if you can, when the light is gentler and the square is quieter. The Sunday artisan market can block parts of the square and put stalls in your frame, so expect a busier picture then. If you want a wider view of the city with the square inside it, Cerro Santa Lucía is an alternative.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de Armas is in the historic centre of Santiago. The Metropolitan Cathedral stands at its north-west corner, and the old colonial government buildings face its north side.
text.directions_text: The Plaza de Armas metro station is under the square, so come up and head for the north-west corner, where the cathedral stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the cathedral façade and the open square in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the monument or the post office dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Catedral Metropolitana de Santiago (front stairways, facing the square from the north side). The cathedral's façade in the foreground with the palm-lined plaza and surrounding colonial buildings opening out behind and around it. For the shot with the cathedral in the foreground, walk to the front stairways of the Catedral Metropolitana de Santiago at the north-west corner. From there you can take in the cathedral façade, the palm-lined plaza and the colonial buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight, so the cathedral does not lean. Put the façade in the foreground and let the palms and the buildings lead the eye across the square. Wait for a few people to cross the plaza to give a sense of scale. For a wider view of the city with the square inside it, try Cerro Santa Lucía instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral stonework to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright sky does not wash out the details. Take a few frames while people walk past.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunny mornings, before the midday crowds. Weekend middays are best avoided, and the Sunday artisan market can fill parts of the square.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship and its opening status can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The square itself is open to walk through without an entry charge.
The cathedral is a place of worship, so visitors should dress and behave respectfully if they go inside.
The metro station under the square has an exit onto the square.

name: San Cristóbal Hill
label: Cerro San Cristóbal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Virgen de la Inmaculada Concepción' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Virgen de la Inmaculada Concepción' (way/1330806606): middle (9 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/285901766: the OpenStreetMap point 'Cerro San Cristóbal'.
notes: Hill topped by the Virgin Mary statue with views over Santiago.

text.description: San Cristóbal Hill (Cerro San Cristóbal) is the big green hill that rises about 300 metres above northern Santiago and tops out at 880 m above sea level. It sits inside the Parque Metropolitano, the city's largest public park. On the summit stands the statue of the Immaculate Conception, 14 metres tall on an 8.3-metre pedestal. It is lit at night, so it can be seen from across the city by day and after dark. That makes it the hill's signature landmark and the best subject for a phone photo here. From the statue's base at the summit you can put the Virgin in the foreground and let Santiago's sprawl and the line of the Andes fill the background, which gives the picture a clear sense of place. Start with the default lens (1x) and the whole scene, then try a closer, tighter shot of the statue against the sky. Late afternoon is the favoured time, when the light warms the statue. If you want a view of the hill itself rather than from it, Parque Bicentenario gives a ground-level look at it rising over the city. For a quieter outlook away from the summit crowds, Mirador El Hundimiento is a lower lookout on the slope. The hill has been in use since 1903, when an observatory was built here, and there is a small chapel inside the pedestal where Pope John Paul II prayed in 1987. It is a place of worship, so keep a respectful distance during services.
text.geographic_location: San Cristóbal Hill is in northern Santiago, rising above Barrio Bellavista and the Chilean National Zoo at its foot. The statue stands on the summit, inside the Parque Metropolitano.
text.directions_text: Without a nearby station to start from, get to Barrio Bellavista by taxi or on foot. It is at the north end of Pío Nono next to the zoo, where the Funicular de Santiago begins. The funicular, or the cable car (Teleférico) from the Oasis station, takes you up to the summit. You can also walk up in about 45 minutes. Check the official site for running times before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the city behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a close, tall shot from the base, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Andes and a tighter crop of the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the statue at the summit, framing it with the city behind). The 14-metre Virgin statue on the summit in the foreground, with Santiago's sprawl and the Andes behind it. For the best shot, go to the base of the statue on the summit, on Virgen de la Inmaculada Concepción, rather than the phone-icon location. From the statue's base the 14-metre Virgin is in the foreground, with Santiago's sprawl and the Andes behind her.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the statue to one side of the frame, using the gridlines, and let the city fill the rest. Crouch a little and tilt the phone up for a stronger, taller statue. If you want the hill itself in the picture, Parque Bicentenario gives a ground-level view of it over the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the statue is not washed out. Use panorama for the sweep of the city, and night mode after dark when the statue is lit.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour before sunset, when the warm light falls on the statue.

text.access_note: The hill is a public park with a sanctuary at the summit, which is a place of worship; the funicular and cable car may have set hours and closures, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts
label: Museo de Bellas Artes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Forestal' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque Forestal' (way/332070819): edge nearest the subject (1225 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/10925461823: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes'.
notes: Neoclassical museum building in Parque Forestal.

text.description: The Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts is one of the main centres for Chilean and wider South American art, and its building is a pleasure to photograph. The museum was founded in 1880, which makes it the oldest of its kind in South America. The palace you see today was opened on 21 September 1910 as part of the celebrations for Chile's first centenary of independence. It was designed by the architect Emile Jéquier in a Beaux-Arts style, with the facade and layout modelled on the Petit Palais in Paris. Behind the grand entrance, the glass cupola over the central hall was made in Belgium and shipped to Chile in 1907. The palace sits inside Parque Forestal, and that setting is what makes the picture. From the open lawns and paths directly across from the front, the whole neoclassical facade fits into one frame, with trees on either side and green space in front. A lagoon once lay in front of the museum, but it was drained in 1944, so there are no reflection shots to hope for. Keep the building centred and the lines straight, because the symmetry is its strongest feature. Walk a few steps left or right to find a gap in the trees that suits you. If you also want a closer shot of the entrance, the pavement and steps in front of the museum work well, but check the official site before you go for any restrictions there.
text.geographic_location: The museum stands inside Parque Forestal in central Santiago. Behind it is the University of Chile's Museum of Contemporary Art.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Parque Forestal in central Santiago. From there the museum is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the full facade with some trees and lawn around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close and cannot fit the building in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the central entrance and the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Forestal (open lawns and paths directly across from the museum's front facade). The museum's neoclassical front facade framed by the trees and open green space of the park. On the open lawns and paths directly across from the museum's front facade. From here the neoclassical front is framed by the park's trees and open green space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the central entrance with the middle vertical line so the symmetry holds. Keep the phone level so the columns and edges do not lean. Let tree branches frame the top or sides of the picture, and keep the lawn or path in the foreground to show the park setting. For a closer alternative, shoot the entrance from the pavement and steps in front of the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If people walk into the frame, take a Live Photo or a short burst and pick the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework and means fewer people on the lawns. Midday sun can flatten the facade.

text.access_note: Parque Forestal is an open public park, but the museum itself and its front steps may have entry rules or restrictions, so check the official site before you go.

sources.title: Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts

name: Gran Torre Santiago
label: Gran Torre Santiago
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1179710949: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gran Torre Costanera' (96 m across).
notes: Tallest building in South America with a top-floor viewing deck.

text.description:
Gran Torre Santiago, also called Gran Torre Costanera or simply "the Costanera" by locals, is the tallest building in South America. It rises 300 metres and has more than 60 storeys. It is part of the Costanera Center complex, which also holds the largest shopping mall in Latin America, two hotels and two other office towers. The design involved Chilean architects Alemparte Barreda & Asociados, the Argentine architect César Pelli and the Canadian company Watt International. Building began in June 2006, was paused in 2009 during the Great Recession, and the tower was completed in 2013. A public observation deck, Sky Costanera, opened on the top floors in 2015.

For a phone photographer the challenge is simple: the tower is huge, so the question is how to fit it in. Standing close to its base, the tall sides draw strong vertical lines up into the sky, and that makes a dramatic picture if you tilt the phone upwards. Take one shot like that, then walk back a little for a second picture showing the whole tower with the sky around it. Switch on the gridlines so the sides of the tower stay straight and the frame feels balanced. Because the complex is a busy place, expect people walking through your foreground; wait a moment for a gap, or use them to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: In Santiago, Chile, as part of the Costanera Center complex, which also includes the large shopping mall and two hotels. The tower is the tallest building in the complex.
text.directions_text: Start from central Santiago and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Costanera Center. The tower is part of that complex, so once you arrive you will be close to it. Follow the map to the tower and then move to the nearest accessible spot around the base. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because from close to the base of the tower it is the only lens that takes in a good length of the building. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for a calmer, less stretched look. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for picking out the top of the tower against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move to the nearest accessible spot around the base to look up at the walls. If you want the whole building in one frame, walk back from there and tilt the phone up.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line one edge of the tower up with a vertical grid line, so the building does not seem to lean. For the upward shot, hold the phone as level as you can and then tilt up only slightly. This keeps the sides from leaning inwards too much. Leave a little sky above the top so the tower does not look cut off.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full-height shot and keep your fingers away from the edges of the lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight with a clear sky gives the cleanest lines. Late afternoon or dusk, when the lights come on, can also work well; if you shoot then, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The tower stands within a busy shopping and office complex; the observation deck is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for access details.

name: La Moneda Palace
label: La Moneda Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Constitución' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Constitución' (way/333850238): middle (200 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/394238: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Presidential Palace of Chile' (170 m across).
notes: Seat of the President of Chile.

text.description:
La Moneda is the working palace of Chile's president, and it fills a whole block of downtown Santiago. It began life as the colonial mint, designed by the Italian architect Joaquín Toesca. Building started in 1784 and it opened in 1805. Coins were struck here until 1929, and the palace became the seat of government in 1845. Today the long, plain, white front is a good example of pure neoclassical style, and its wide, horizontal shape reads clearly even on a small phone screen.

It photographs well because the square in front gives the building room. A statue-lined forecourt leads the eye towards the façade, so you can fit the whole front in one frame without stepping back into traffic. Plaza de la Constitución was laid out in 1930, and it is the best-known angle on the north side. You can't get close to the palace itself, as it is gated and guarded, so plan for a wide shot from the square rather than details.

If you can, time your visit for the changing of the guard. It is a formal ceremony dating back to the 1850s, with a band and mounted troops. Dates and times vary between guides, so check the schedule before you go. Keep a little space around you for people, and expect security staff to ask you to move away from the entrances.
text.geographic_location: La Moneda is in the Civic District of downtown Santiago, in a block bordered by Moneda street to the north, Morandé to the east, the Alameda to the south and Teatinos to the west.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for the Civic District in downtown Santiago and ask for Plaza de la Constitución, in front of the palace. Once you are the palace lies to the south and is about 2 minutes on foot away. You don't need to walk any closer for the main view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the full front doesn't fit, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for flags, statues and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Constitución (north side, facing the main façade). The full white façade of the palace across the open forecourt, with the statues in the foreground framing the approach. On the north side, facing the main façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the palace along the lower or middle line, keeping the roofline level. Include a statue or two at the edge to add depth. For a different view, try the clear, frontal angle from Plaza de la Ciudadanía, or look down the tree-lined Paseo Bulnes, where the street leads the eye to the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white walls keep their detail rather than turning flat and bright. Take a Live Photo or a short video during the changing of the guard.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for soft light, or evening when the palace is lit. A late-afternoon golden hour also works. The view is at its liveliest during the changing of the guard, so check the day and time before you go.

text.access_note: The surrounding plazas are open public space, but the palace itself is gated and guarded, and security may limit photography near the entrances or during sensitive events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Because the main front faces north, a visitor standing in front is likely to have the sun more or less behind them for much of the day, which tends to light the façade well.
A white façade can look overexposed in bright light, so lowering the exposure slightly usually helps.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects at the edges of the frame, so keep the palace towards the middle.

name: Santa Lucía Hill
label: Santa Lucía Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terraza Neptuno' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Terraza Neptuno' (relation/15512515): middle (97 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/314997482: the OpenStreetMap point 'Cerro Santa Lucía'.
notes: Small hill park with terraces, castle-like fort and city views.

text.description:
Santa Lucía Hill rises in the middle of Santiago as a small, green island of stairways, terraces and fountains. The park covers about 65,300 square metres, and the hill stands 69 metres above the streets around it. Much of its look comes from a big remodelling in 1872 led by Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, which gave it the yellow and white facades, the winding road and the summit chapel. Pedro de Valdivia took the hill in 1540, and the old Fort Hidalgo, finished in 1820, still gives it a castle-like feel. A cannon is traditionally fired at noon.

For a phone photo, start at the lower terraces by the Neptune Fountain. The fountain sits in the foreground and the green, staired slopes climb behind it, so you get water, stone and plants in one frame. It is an easy first stop before you climb. Higher up, the summit has a viewpoint, but smog can hide the Andes on many days, so treat distant mountains as a bonus. If you want a second picture, the ornate stone gateway at the foot of the hill and the walls and towers of Castillo Hidalgo both make good, historic-looking backdrops. Keep your belongings secure while you take photos, as one reviewer reported people posing as tourists near the top.
text.geographic_location: Santa Lucía Hill is in the centre of Santiago. It lies between Alameda del Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins to the south, Santa Lucía Street to the west and Victoria Subercaseaux to the east.
text.directions_text: Head for the Alameda del Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins in central Santiago. The ornate gateway is reported to be near the Alameda corner; confirm the exact gate on arrival. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the slopes behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the fountain and stairs will not fit, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details and the facades higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terraza Neptuno (lower terraces, at the Fuente de Neptuno). The Neptune Fountain in the foreground with the green, staired slopes of the hill rising behind it. Face the hill, which is to the north, and the fountain fills the foreground with the green, staired slopes rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the fountain on the lower third, leaving the stairs and greenery above it. Keep your phone level so the steps do not lean. For a different view, try the stone gateway at the foot of the hill or the walls and towers of Castillo Hidalgo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer, according to one photo guide.

text.access_note: The hill is a public park, but part of the climb has been reported closed for maintenance and the park closes in the evening, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the fountain and the stairs into one frame when you are standing close.
Lowering the exposure slider and using a Live Photo suit a bright, watery scene like the fountain.
The gateway at the foot of the hill is reported to be near the Alameda corner; confirm the exact gate on arrival.
Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light (from one photo guide).
Part of the climb has been reported closed for maintenance, and the park closes in the evening (reviewer reports).

name: La Chascona
label: La Chascona
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'La Chascona' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1214175916: the OpenStreetMap point 'Casa Museo La Chascona'.
notes: Pablo Neruda's house in Bellavista.

text.description: La Chascona is the Santiago house of the poet Pablo Neruda, in Barrio Bellavista. From the pavement, what catches the eye is the bright blue painted entrance wall, with a sunflower-face sign reading La Chascona and the front door just beside it. That blue and the sign are the most recognisable parts of the outside, and you can photograph them from the public pavement without going in. Building began in 1953, when the house was meant as a home for Matilde Urrutia, Neruda's secret lover at the time. She later became his third wife. The name refers to her curly red hair: 'chascona' is a Chilean Spanish word meaning tangled hair. After Neruda died in 1973 the house was damaged during the military coup, and Urrutia restored it. It is now a museum. The street is a quiet backstreet. Start with the blue wall and sign filling the frame, then shuffle sideways to include the door. A second, wider shot along Fernando Márquez de la Plata shows the painted wall and facade on a calm Bellavista backstreet, with the hill of San Cristóbal rising behind. Rules about photography inside the museum are not clear, so keep your phone for the outside unless staff tell you otherwise, and check the museum's current rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Barrio Bellavista, Santiago, on Fernando Márquez de la Plata, with San Cristóbal hill visible rising behind the house along the street.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops right at this spot, so navigate to Fernando Márquez de la Plata 192 in the Bellavista district around the house. The house is on the street itself, so the phone icon on the map is right at the entrance wall. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the blue wall and sign together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole facade in frame, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the bright blue entrance wall, the sunflower-face sign reading La Chascona and the front door in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the sign on one of the upper intersections, with the door in the lower part of the frame. For a different view, walk a little way along Fernando Márquez de la Plata and photograph the painted wall and facade down the quiet backstreet, with San Cristóbal hill behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blue wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the blue looks washed out or the sky is bright. Use 2x zoom to tighten the framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft and the pavement is not busy with visitors; a quieter moment lets you shoot without people in the frame.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public pavement, but entry to the museum and its photography rules may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Santiago Metropolitan Cathedral
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Armas' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Armas' (node/6231367141): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q15042373: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neoclassical cathedral on the Plaza de Armas.

text.description:
Santiago's cathedral is the main Catholic church in Chile and the seat of the Archbishop of Santiago. It is dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin Mary and stands facing the Plaza de Armas, together with the Archbishop's Palace and the Parish del Sagrario. All of these buildings are national monuments. The present church is the fifth on this site. It was built between 1748 and 1906, to designs linked with Joaquín Toesca and Ignacio Cremonesi, and Toesca gave the facade its neoclassical look.

It photographs well because the plaza gives you room to step back. From the open square you can fit the whole neoclassical facade into one frame, with the plaza's trees and the older buildings around it adding depth and a sense of place. The mix of architectural styles around the square makes the scene feel busy but still readable.

For your phone, stand in the plaza in front of the main facade and take a wide shot first, then move closer for details. Morning light is said to suit the facade's details, and dusk can add a warmer tone. If you have time, Cerro Santa Lucía is suggested for a view over the city with the cathedral in the foreground, and Parque Forestal for other angles. Check the sightlines when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the commune of Santiago, on the side of the Plaza de Armas. The Archbishop's Palace and the Parish del Sagrario form part of the same architectural ensemble.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaza de Armas in central Santiago. The cathedral faces the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole facade and the open plaza. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the front. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the details of the facade and the upper parts of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Armas (in front of the cathedral's main facade). The neoclassical facade framed by the open plaza, with the square's trees and surrounding historic buildings in view. In front of the cathedral's main facade. From here the neoclassical facade is framed by the open plaza, with the square's trees and the surrounding historic buildings in view. The cathedral lies to the south-west of the point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the facade's vertical lines straight, with the towers lined up with the grid. Use a tree or a part of the plaza as a natural frame at one side. Hold the phone level to stop the building leaning. For a different view, Cerro Santa Lucía is said to give a city panorama with the cathedral in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its detail. If you step inside, switch off the flash, as it may be restricted.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is said to suit the facade's details. One guide suggests dusk for golden light.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so be respectful of worshippers inside and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

name: Barrio Lastarria
label: Barrio Lastarria
camera_source: Commons cluster (49 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1496201363: large area 'Barrio Lastarria' (803 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Bohemian neighbourhood with cafés, murals and small plazas.

text.description: Barrio Lastarria is a historical neighbourhood in the middle of Santiago, and it is a good place to photograph everyday city life rather than one big monument. Its winding streets are lined with cafés, cinemas, theatres and museums, and there is often something going on outdoors, such as a festival or a live performance. The neighbourhood grew up around the Iglesia de la Veracruz, a neoclassical church from 1857, and the church's facades were restored in 2001 and 2002. Plaza Mulato Gil de Castro was laid out in 1981 to protect a row of older frontages beside the early 19th-century Gil de Castro house. Chile gave the whole area official protected status as a Zona Típica in 1997, so many of the old streets have kept their character. Because the area is wide, no single frame sums it up. Take a few pictures instead: a street scene with café tables, a close-up of a colourful facade, the church front, and a view along a leafy street toward Santa Lucía Hill. Parque Forestal, on the northern edge, is a pleasant break between shots. Keep a little distance from people at café tables, and wipe your lens before you start, as phone lenses pick up smudges easily.
text.geographic_location: Barrio Lastarria is in central Santiago, between Parque Forestal to the north and the Alameda and Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral to the south. Santa Lucía Hill lies to its west and Plaza Baquedano to its east.
text.directions_text: The Metro stations Universidad Católica and Bellas Artes both give direct access to the neighbourhood. From either one, walk into the streets between Santa Lucía Hill and Parque Forestal and head for the middle of the district. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, head for Parque Forestal or Plaza Baquedano and continue on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most street scenes, as it looks natural and copes well with cafés and passers-by. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow lanes or the church front when you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as facades, signs and balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Face south-west, take one frame from where you are, then wander a few streets in any direction for others, because the area is wide and has no single viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the street so it leads the eye into the picture, with the buildings on both sides roughly straight. Include a few people or café tables to give a sense of scale and life. Hold the phone level to keep vertical lines upright, especially at 0.5x. Look for a clear foreground, such as a table or a plant pot, and let the facades fill the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or a wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright facades don't wash out. Use portrait mode for close-ups of cafés, food or flowers, and try a Live Photo on a lively street corner to capture movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets. After dusk, lit-up café streets look good in night mode, as long as you hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The neighbourhood is made up of open public streets and squares; individual museums, theatres and the church may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets.
Lit-up café streets look good in night mode after dusk.
The streets are narrow in places, so ultra-wide (0.5x) helps.
There are café tables outdoors that can be used as foreground.

name: Plaza Baquedano
label: Plaza Baquedano
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Baquedano' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Baquedano' (way/26103793): middle (251 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26103793: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Plaza Baquedano' (251 m across).
notes: Central roundabout also known as Plaza Italia, Santiago's gathering point.

text.description: Plaza Baquedano, which most people in Santiago call Plaza Italia, is an oval square where several of the city's main avenues meet: Providencia, the Alameda and Vicuña Mackenna. It was laid out in 1875 as Plaza La Serena and took its present name in 1928, when the monument to General Manuel Baquedano, made by the Chilean sculptor Virgínio Arias, was put up. It stands where the Mapocho River once forked, and Parque Forestal, Balmaceda Park and Bustamante Park all meet here. It photographs well because you can show the monument, the converging avenues and the city traffic in one frame, and a wider shot shows how the square links the centre, Providencia and Bellavista. The square has also been the focus of celebrations and protests, and in 2019–2021 protesters called it Plaza de la Dignidad. The four-ton statue was taken away in March 2021 to be restored, so check whether it is back before building a photo around it. If it is not, the square and the avenues still make the shot. Expect plenty of traffic and, at times, crowds or demonstrations. Keep your phone close and watch the road when you step back for a wide view.
text.geographic_location: Plaza Baquedano is at the meeting point of central Santiago and the Providencia district, next to Parque Forestal and Bustamante Park. Bellavista is close by.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so start from the city centre or from Providencia and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Plaza Baquedano (Plaza Italia). The centre is about 19 m (roughly 20-25 steps) to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole square and the avenues, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Baquedano (on the square, close to the equestrian statue of General Baquedano). The bronze equestrian statue of General Manuel Baquedano framed against the converging avenues and the city traffic around the roundabout. The centre is roughly 20-25 steps to the west. The statue of General Baquedano was removed in March 2021, so it may not be in place. If it is back, frame the bronze horse and rider against the avenues that meet at the roundabout. If it is missing, frame the avenues and the traffic moving around the square instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines. If the statue is back, put it on one of the lines, with an avenue running away behind it; otherwise use an avenue or the monument's plinth as the anchor. Take a closer shot of the monument, then step back and use 0.5x for a wider view that shows how the square links the centre, Providencia and Bellavista. For a quieter, higher view, Mirador Hundimiento looks down over the city toward Plaza Baquedano and the Telefónica tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Use night mode for evening shots and rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives the statue stronger relief. In the evening you can include the lit-up streets around the square.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space with no charge, but it is surrounded by traffic and has seen demonstrations; if you plan to use Mirador Hundimiento, check the hill's access hours and any lookout charges before you go.

name: Iglesia de San Francisco
label: San Francisco Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cerro Santa Lucía' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cerro Santa Lucía' (way/23321628): middle (530 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/114621538: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de San Francisco' (82 m across).
notes: Oldest surviving colonial church in Santiago.

text.description:
The Iglesia de San Francisco is a Franciscan church on Avenida Libertador General Bernardo O'Higgins, in downtown Santiago. It is one of the oldest colonial-era buildings in Chile. It was consecrated in 1622 and has come through about 15 earthquakes of magnitude over 7. The first bell tower fell in an earthquake in 1647. The tower you see today was built in the mid-1800s to a design by Fermín Vivaceta, and its clock is a distinctive feature. Part of the old convent next door is now the Museo Colonial.

For a photo with a different angle from the usual street-level facade, look down on the church from Cerro Santa Lucía. From the upper paths of the hill, the bell tower sits among the downtown streets and the Alameda, so you get the church in its city setting.

If you want the facade as well, the church shows its full baroque west front, with columns, statues and carvings, from the open plaza in front. Take both shots if you have time. Start on the hill for the tower and the view, then walk down for the detail close up. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the tower does not lean in your picture.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Santiago, on Avenida Libertador General Bernardo O'Higgins (the Alameda), beside the old convent that now houses the Museo Colonial. The viewpoint, Cerro Santa Lucía, lies to the north-east of the church.
text.directions_text: Cerro Santa Lucía is in central Santiago and can be reached on foot. The church is about 550 m to the south-west of that point. Once you are at the church, the plaza in front of it is the place for the facade photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from the hill to pick out the bell tower and its clock. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider view of the tower among the streets. At the plaza in front of the church, use ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the whole facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cerro Santa Lucía (upper paths of the hill, looking down toward the church). The church's bell tower seen from above, set within the downtown streets and the Alameda. From there the church lies to the south-west. You will be looking down on the bell tower, with the downtown streets and the Alameda around it. For the facade, walk to the open plaza in front of the church and shoot the west front head-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the hill, zoom in so the tower fills about a third of the frame, and leave the rooftops and the line of the Alameda in the lower part of the picture. Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line. At the plaza, step back as far as you can and tilt the phone as little as possible to keep the columns straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. At 3x or 5x, hold the phone with both hands, or brace it against a wall or railing, to keep the image sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when soft light is said to suit the tower from the hill. The plaza facade may look best in even daylight.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any photo rules. Also check access to Cerro Santa Lucía before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The upper paths of Cerro Santa Lucía look down towards the church and its bell tower.
Soft light at sunrise or sunset suits photographs of the bell tower.
The hill may have its own access rules or opening hours.
The church may restrict photography inside, and visitors are normally expected to dress modestly.
Cerro Santa Lucía can be reached on foot from central Santiago.

name: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
label: Precolumbian Art Museu
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1297763053: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museum of Precolombian Art'.
notes: Museum of pre-Columbian art in the old Royal Customs House.

text.description: The Chilean Museum of Pre-Columbian Art fills the old Palacio de la Real Aduana, a building put up between 1805 and 1807. It stands a block west of the Plaza de Armas, close to the Palacio de los Tribunales de Justicia and the Former National Congress Building, so it is easy to add to a walk round the historic centre. The museum opened in December 1981. It was founded by the architect and collector Sergio Larraín García-Moreno to show the pre-Columbian pieces he had gathered over nearly fifty years. In January 2014 a new phase by the architect Smiljan Radić Clarke increased the area by about 70%. Inside, there are more than 3,000 pieces from almost 100 different peoples, spanning roughly 10,000 years. For a phone photographer, the appeal is an early nineteenth-century public building in the middle of a busy city. Start with a straight-on shot of the entrance, then look for angles that show the building's age against the modern street. The default lens (1x) gives the most natural view. If you want the full width of the front, try the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep your phone level so the walls do not lean. Pedestrians pass constantly, so wait a moment for a clear frame. Photography rules inside the galleries may differ from those outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Santiago, one block west of the Plaza de Armas. It is close to the Palacio de los Tribunales de Justicia and the Former National Congress Building.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot. The museum is one block west of the Plaza de Armas, so start from the plaza and head west for one block. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so you do not need to walk further once you reach it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the entrance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole front in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for doorway and stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the front of the building up with them so the vertical edges stay straight. Take one wide shot to show the whole building, then a closer one of the entrance. Tap the building to set focus and slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the building and use the exposure slider to stop the sky washing out. If people walk through the frame, take a Live Photo and pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the street is quieter, such as early in the day, for fewer people in the frame. Soft daylight is kinder to the stonework than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: This is a museum in a historic building; the outside can be photographed from the street, but entry and any photography inside may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Parque Forestal
label: Parque Forestal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puente Patronato' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Puente Patronato' (way/23393550): middle (46 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/332070819: large area 'Parque Forestal' (1225 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Long tree-lined park along the Mapocho river.

text.description: Parque Forestal is a long, green strip of park in the historical downtown of Santiago, laid out on land reclaimed from the Mapocho River. It sits west of Plaza Baquedano and east of Estación Mapocho, with Santa María Avenue on its north side and Merced Street on its south. One of its distinctive features is its three lines of plane trees (platanus orientalis), which make long, repeating rows of trunks and leafy shade. That repetition is what photographs well on a phone: paths that lead the eye into the distance, with the river running alongside. The park also holds the National Museum of Fine Arts, which shares a building with the Santiago Museum of Contemporary Art. Palacio Bruna stands opposite on Merced Street. At its eastern end the park carries on as Balmaceda Park, so the greenery runs on almost unbroken along the river. For the best overview, take your photo from Puente Patronato, where you can see the tree-lined paths and the Mapocho together. If you want a second angle, try the corner of Merced and Coronel Santiago Bueras, where the view looks across the treetops toward the downtown skyline. Keep people in the frame if you can. A walker or cyclist on the path gives a good sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Parque Forestal is in the historical downtown of Santiago, between Plaza Baquedano to the east and Estación Mapocho to the west. It lies along the Mapocho River, between Santa María Avenue and Merced Street.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the well-known area around Plaza Baquedano or Estación Mapocho, which lie at either end of the park. From there, Parque Forestal is about 460 m to the south-east, roughly 5-6 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the paths and river as you see them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the tree rows in the frame, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to compress the trees into a tighter pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Puente Patronato. Tree-lined park paths and the Mapocho river running alongside them, seen from the bridge. From the bridge you see the tree-lined paths with the Mapocho river running beside them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the river or the nearest path with one of the lines, so the rows of trees lead into the distance. Keep the bridge railing out of the corners, or use it deliberately as a foreground edge. For a different view, walk to Merced and Coronel Santiago Bueras for a wider look across the treetops toward the downtown skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest patch of foliage to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and leaves don't wash out. If a walker or cyclist passes, a Live Photo lets you pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not directly overhead, so the trees give softer light and less harsh shadow on the paths. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The park itself is an open public space, but if you want to go into the National Museum of Fine Arts, check the official site before you go.

name: Barrio Bellavista
label: Barrio Bellavista
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Camilo Mori' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Plazuela Camilo Mori' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/847467331: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bellavista de San Cristóbal'.
notes: Colourful street-art quarter at the foot of Cerro San Cristóbal.

text.description:
Barrio Bellavista is Santiago's bohemian quarter, a neighbourhood dating from 1900 that sits between the Mapocho River and San Cristóbal Hill. It is full of restaurants, galleries, bars and boutiques, and many of the city's intellectuals and artists live here. Pablo Neruda's Santiago house, La Chascona, is in the district too. It photographs well because the colour comes from the streets themselves: murals, café fronts and old façades, all close together and easy to walk between.

The best single place to start is Plaza Camilo Mori, off Pío Nono, in the heart of the neighbourhood. At one end stands the large red Castillo Lehuedé (the Castillo Rojo), a 1923 building that gives you a strong, recognisable backdrop for the whole barrio. Keep it to one side of the frame and let the plaza and the people in it fill the rest, so the picture shows the neighbourhood and not just the building.

If you have time, walk a little way to Pío Nono for a long view down the main street, with graffiti, murals and cafés in the foreground. Terraza Bellavista gives a raised view over the barrio and the city towards the Andes. Street art on Constitución, Antonia López de Bello and Dardignac changes often, so what you see may differ from older photos. On weekends an evening handicrafts market runs along Pío Nono, which adds life to your pictures.
text.geographic_location: Bellavista lies in Santiago between the Mapocho River and San Cristóbal Hill, in the communes of Providencia and Recoleta. Plaza Camilo Mori is beside the Teatro Mori, just off the main street, Pío Nono.
text.directions_text: The Baquedano Metro station lies across the river to the south of the neighbourhood. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the plaza to fit the Castillo Rojo and the street life around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the red building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for mural details and café fronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Camilo Mori (off Pío Nono, in the heart of the neighbourhood). The plaza with the large red Castillo Lehuedé (Castillo Rojo) at one end, framing the bohemian streetscape around it. Plaza Camilo Mori is the nearby viewpoint, with the red Castillo Lehuedé at one end of the plaza. From the plaza you can frame the castle and the bohemian streets around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the red building's edges straight against them. Leave some plaza and people in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different view, try Pío Nono for a long shot down the street, or Terraza Bellavista for a wider view over the barrio towards the Andes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red façade to set focus, then nudge the exposure slider down slightly so the colour stays rich and the sky does not wash out. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is easiest for murals and the red building. A weekend evening is livelier, with the handicrafts market along Pío Nono, but you will want night mode for photos then.

text.access_note: The plaza and streets are open public space; if you plan to use the funicular to reach Terraza Bellavista, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Daytime light is easier for photographing murals and façades than evening light.
Evening photos in the barrio will usually need night mode.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep a bright red façade from washing out.

name: Funicular de Santiago
label: Funicular
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Estación Pío Nono' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Pío Nono' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Historic funicular railway up Cerro San Cristóbal.

text.description:
The Funicular de Santiago is a short railway that climbs the slope of Cerro San Cristóbal, part of Santiago Metropolitan Park. The best photo is at the base station, Estación Pío Nono. There the red car waits at the platform in front of the old stone station building, and the track rises up the hillside behind it. The colours work well together: red car, grey stone and green slope.

The line is 485 metres long and has three stations: Pío Nono at the bottom, Zoo, and Cumbre at the top, where the Santuario a la Virgen stands. It opened on 25 April 1925, and architect Luciano Kulczewski designed the station at the foot of the hill. Pope John Paul II rode it during his 1987 visit, and it became a National Monument of Chile in 2000.

For a phone photo, keep it simple. Stand at the platform, line up the car and the station front, and let the track lead the eye upwards. Turn on gridlines so the building stays straight. If the platform is busy, wait a moment for a gap, then take a few shots in a row. Photos from inside the station may depend on the ticket and the day, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: At the foot of Cerro San Cristóbal, inside Santiago Metropolitan Park, at the Pío Nono base station on Calle Pío Nono.
text.directions_text: Head for the foot of Cerro San Cristóbal in Santiago and look for Pío Nono 450, where the base station stands. Use a map app to navigate to Pío Nono 450. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the car, the platform and the stone station building together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the platform is too tight to fit the building in. Use 2x if you want the car and the track without the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base station, Pío Nono 450, facing the platform). The red funicular car at the platform in front of the historic stone station building, with the hillside track rising behind it. From here you see the red funicular car at the platform in front of the historic stone building, with the hillside track rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the car slightly off-centre and let the track climb through the upper part of the frame. Switch on gridlines and keep the station front level with the lines. For a different view, Cerro Santa Lucía gives a distant view across the city of the track climbing the wooded slope. Use the telephoto (2x-5x) there, as the track will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red car to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the car colour stays rich. Take a Live Photo if the car is about to move off, then choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the platform is quiet so you can get the car without people in front. Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the stone and the red paint, but check the official site for running times before you go.

text.access_note: The base station is part of a tourist attraction in Santiago Metropolitan Park, so entry and tickets may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral
label: Centro GAM
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cerro Santa Lucía' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cerro Santa Lucía' (way/23321628): middle (530 m across).

notes: Large cultural centre with a striking rusted-steel facade.

text.description: The Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral, usually called the GAM, is a cultural centre on Avenida Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins. It was built for a major international conference in 1972 and finished in just 275 days, with thousands of volunteers helping. It later served as a military headquarters, and a fire in 2006 led to its return to cultural use. It opened as the GAM in September 2010 and now hosts drama, dance, music and visual arts. For photographs, its best feature is the rusty-brown corten steel facade with angled, perforated panels, which gives plenty of texture and pattern. This map suggests two ways to shoot it. Close up, stand on the avenue and photograph the facade straight on. From there you look out over the city centre and its skyline, with the GAM among the buildings below to the east. It is a quieter, higher alternative to street level. How clearly the GAM shows depends on exactly where you stand at the top, so check the framing on your screen before you take the shot. Zoom in to pick out the building, and use the skyline around it to give a sense of place.
text.geographic_location: The GAM is in central Santiago, on Avenida Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Cerro Santa Lucía in the city centre. From the summit viewpoint, the GAM lies about 350 m to the east if you want to continue to the building itself. It stands on Avenida Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins, at number 227. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the skyline and the layout of the city. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the GAM below. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the sweep of the hilltop and city.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cerro Santa Lucía (summit viewpoint at the top of the hill). A wide elevated view over central Santiago and its skyline, with the GAM visible in the city below; the sources do not confirm how clearly it is framed. Face east over the city centre and look for the GAM among the buildings below. Move a few steps along the lookout if trees or rooftops block the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line, so the city fills most of the picture. Zoom in with the telephoto lens until the GAM is clear, with some skyline around it. For close-up shots of the corten steel facade and its perforated panels, you can also photograph the building straight on from the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the GAM on the screen to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't turn into a silhouette. Hold your phone steady against a wall or railing when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is a good choice, when the sun is behind you as you look east and the light is softer. Check the framing on site, because the view may change with the season and the weather.

text.access_note: Cerro Santa Lucía is a free, open-air hill and the GAM's public spaces are free to walk through, but some performances need tickets, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light falls from the west, so looking east from the summit puts the sun behind the photographer.
Trees or rooftops may block parts of the view of the GAM from the summit lookout, depending on where you stand.
Zooming in on a phone helps pick out a distant building, and bracing the phone on a wall or railing reduces shake.

name: Torre Entel
label: Torre Entel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Forestal' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque Forestal' (way/332070819): edge nearest the subject (1225 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/462866500: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre Entel' (23 m across).
notes: Telecommunications tower, a landmark of the skyline.

text.description:
Torre Entel is a slim concrete telecommunications tower, 127.4 metres tall, with a shape meant to recall a torch. Building began in 1970 and it was inaugurated in 1974. For many years it was the tallest structure in Chile. Taller buildings have since overtaken it, but it still stands out on the Santiago skyline and is a familiar sight on postcards. In 2009 a very large LED screen was added at the top, so the crown of the tower can look different from one visit to the next.

The tower is only moderately photogenic on its own, so the framing matters. The Parque Forestal view works well because the tower rises above the trees and the greenery gives the picture a natural border. A simple, calm shot, with leaves at the edges and the tower as the single tall shape, usually beats a crowded wide view. If you want a different angle, Plaza de la Ciudadanía gives an open view of the whole tower, and Cerro Santa Lucía shows it among the city rooftops from higher up.

You are a fair way from the tower at the park, so expect to zoom. Keep the tower upright and centred, and leave a little sky above it. You do not need to go up the tower for any of these pictures.
text.geographic_location: Torre Entel stands in central Santiago, beside Avenida Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins (the Alameda) and about a block from La Moneda Palace. Parque Forestal, the park for this view, lies to the north-east of the tower.
text.directions_text: For the tower itself, the area around La Moneda Palace is the easiest starting point, and the Santiago Metro's La Moneda station is right beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant tower closer. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you want more trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Forestal. The tower rising above the trees, framed by the park's greenery. Face south-west and look for the tower rising above the treetops, framed by the park's greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Let branches and leaves form a loose border at the top or sides, and keep the tower upright and near the centre. Turn on gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. For another angle, try Plaza de la Ciudadanía for an open view of the whole tower, or Cerro Santa Lucía for a view with the skyline around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in, and take a few frames to choose from.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the tower is easier to separate from the sky. At dusk, the lit screen at the top may add some interest.

text.access_note: The tower's observation deck may not be open to visitors, so check the official site before you go if you want to go up.
claims_not_in_sources: Parque Forestal lies to the north-east of the tower.
From a distance of over a kilometre, the telephoto lens helps bring the tower closer.
Morning or late afternoon light is softer and separates the tower from the sky better.
The lit LED screen at the top of the tower may add interest at dusk.

name: Palacio Cousiño
label: Palacio Cousiño
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Dieciocho' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Dieciocho nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/180191376: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palacio Cousiño' (62 m across).
notes: Opulent 19th-century mansion museum.

text.description: Palacio Cousiño is a grand palace on Dieciocho Street, built for Isidora Goyenechea, the widow of Luis Cousiño. It was designed by the architect Paul Lathoud in the Second Empire style and finished in 1878. The two-storey front is symmetrical, with ornamental detail, railings and decorative tilework, so it suits a straight-on, tidy photograph. From the street you can take in the whole facade in one frame, and the repeating windows and railings give the picture a pleasing rhythm. The palace was damaged in the 2010 earthquake and reopened in 2015, so check for closures before you travel. The garden and mosaics you may see in other people's photos are inside the grounds, so don't count on them from the pavement. Visits inside are by guided tour, and photography indoors is usually not allowed, so plan to get your best pictures outside. Stand across the street from the entrance at number 438, hold the phone level and let the gridlines help you keep the symmetry. If you can't fit the whole front in, step back or switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone upright to avoid leaning walls. Plaza Las Heras is suggested as a second view of the eastern side of the building, with its metal winter garden and blue-tinted glass, but check on the day.
text.geographic_location: The palace is at 438 Dieciocho Street in Santiago, Chile.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for Dieciocho Street in Santiago and look for number 438. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and the telephoto (2x or more) for railings and tile details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Dieciocho (across the street from the main facade, at the entrance (Dieciocho 438)). The symmetrical two-storey main facade with its ornamental details, railings and decorative tilework, framed from the street. Across the street from the main facade, at the entrance (Dieciocho 438).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central axis of the building up with the middle vertical line, so both sides look balanced. Hold the phone upright and level to keep the walls straight. For a different view, Plaza Las Heras is suggested for the eastern side of the building, where the blue-tinted glass of the metal winter garden may show against the house, but check on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the details of the tilework and railings stay clear. Take a wide shot and a close-up of the decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder than harsh midday sun, and traffic or passers-by are easier to avoid when the street is quiet.

text.access_note: The palace is visited on guided tours and may charge an entry fee, so check the official site before you go; the street view of the facade is from a public pavement.

name: Mercado Central de Santiago
label: Mercado Central
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mercado Central' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of San Pablo and Puente (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1335395103: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mercado Central'.
notes: Iron-framed fish market with famous seafood restaurants.

text.description:
The Mercado Central is Santiago's central market, and from the street it looks like a grand, calm civic building, with a neoclassical front, an archway and a pediment. It fills a whole city block, so the best exterior photo is taken from the street corner, where the whole front fits into one frame with passers-by walking through the foreground. That gives your picture a sense of scale and everyday city life.

The market opened in 1872, with Fermín Vivaceta in charge of construction. It replaced the Plaza del Abasto, which a fire destroyed in 1864. The real showpiece is inside: a cast-iron roof made by the Scottish firm R Laidlaw & Sons in Glasgow. A central pyramidal roof topped by a domed tower rises over eight smaller two-tier roofs, all enclosed by a masonry building.

Start outside for the facade, then go in for the ironwork. Under the roof you can look up at the trusses and the central lantern above the fish stalls, and the water-carrier statue in front of the lattice ironwork makes a good second subject. Entrances get busy, so stand to one side and keep your phone close rather than holding it out at arm's length. Ask vendors before taking close-up shots of them or their stalls. Early morning is said to give the best light.
text.geographic_location: In central Santiago, on a full city block between San Pablo and Puente streets. The market's address is San Pablo 967.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the centre of Santiago and walk or use local transport to the market at San Pablo 967. From there the market's main building is about 90 m to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole facade, and use telephoto (2x or more) for the archway and pediment detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of San Pablo and Puente (outside the building, along the neoclassical facade where the block fronts the two streets). The market's neoclassical exterior with its archway and pediment, with pedestrians in the foreground. The market lies to the north-east, so turn that way. From here you can frame the archway and pediment together, with pedestrians in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the archway near the centre so the pediment sits level at the top. Let a few people walk through the lower part of the frame for scale. Inside, a second option is to stand in the middle of the hall and shoot upwards at the pyramidal roof trusses and central lantern above the fish stalls. A third is the water-carrier statue against the lattice ironwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky doesn't wash out the pediment. Indoors, hold the phone steady and use night mode only if the hall is dim. Keep the phone close to you in the busy entrances.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is said to give the best light, and it is also a good time to photograph before the entrances get busy.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the street, but it is a working market, so check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements.

name: Estación Mapocho
label: Estación Mapocho
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Cultura' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Cultura' (way/122150897): middle (106 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24964200: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Centro Cultural Estación Mapocho' (192 m across).
notes: Former railway station turned cultural centre with a grand iron-and-glass hall.

text.description:
Estación Mapocho is a former railway station in central Santiago that now works as a cultural centre. The design began in 1905 under the architect Emilio Jecquier. The building is about 280 metres long and 17 metres high, with a masonry base and a steel vault that was once glazed and is now covered in copper. It was inaugurated in May 1912 and opened to the public in 1913, as part of Chile's celebrations of its first hundred years of independence. It was declared a National Monument in 1976, and since March 1994 it has hosted exhibitions, concerts and the yearly Santiago International Book Fair.

It works well on a phone because the brick front and the long copper roof make a strong, simple shape, and the open Plaza de la Cultura gives you room to stand back. The paving in the plaza is part of the picture, so let it fill the bottom of the frame. Street vendors often gather in front of the building, so wait a moment for a clear view or include them as a bit of local life. If you have time, the view along Avenida Santa María shows the dome and roofline over the river. Check the angle on the map first.
text.geographic_location: Estación Mapocho stands on the south bank of the Mapocho River, at the corner of Avenida Presidente Balmaceda and Bandera, close to the Mercado Central. The Plaza de la Cultura is the open square in front of it.
text.directions_text: Puente Cal y Canto metro station lies beneath the Plaza de la Cultura, so you come up into the square in front of the building. If you are coming from elsewhere in Santiago, go by taxi to Plaza de la Cultura. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long front of the building into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) when you have stepped back, for less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the brickwork, the arch and the copper roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Cultura (in front of the main facade, on the south side of the building). The Beaux Arts front of the station straight on, with its brick facade and copper roof framed by the paved plaza. From here you look along the brick front and copper roof, which stretch away to the west. For a straight-on view of the facade, walk west along the plaza towards the middle of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't tilt. Keep the phone level and at chest height to avoid leaning walls. Let some of the plaza paving fill the bottom of the picture. For a second view, try Avenida Santa María, where the dome and roofline appear over the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the roof and sky keep their detail. Take a panorama only if you cannot fit the building in with the ultra-wide.

text.access_note: The plaza and the outside of the building are open public space, but exhibitions and some areas inside may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
